title: Defining Aging Across Living and Non-Living Systems
content: Aging is a universal concept across complex systems. Like entropy, aging is anthropomorphic in that it belongs to the system specified by chosen defining properties rather than to a physical object. To understand aging from first principles, we reviewed definitions of aging and equivalent terms in 415 living and non-living systems and found that nearly all tie the change of a property to an internal state that changes with time, use or exposure. Adding the direction that separates aging from development and recovery, we define aging as the cumulative drift of a system’s internal state towards the boundary of the region of state space in which its defining emergent properties persist. Aging is therefore an emergent property of a complex system, and once the system is chosen, its dynamics decide whether and how fast it ages. A system can age only if regulation and renewal leave some slowly changing variable unrestored. Of four cases of drift towards a boundary, only weakening regulation both slows recovery from a small challenge and enlarges the response. For organisms, with death as the boundary and the distance from death as reserve, the definition specifies what biomarkers must track, rejuvenation must restore and negligible senescence must preserve.
